paper_a.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho, Jain, Abbeel, 2020)

paper_b.title: Score-Based Generative Modeling through SDEs (Song et al., 2020)

metadata.description: DDPM and Score-SDE are shown by the latter paper to be equivalent formulations of the same underlying generative process. DDPM works in discrete time (T steps of Gaussian noise addition/removal); Score-SDE reveals that DDPM is a discretization of a variance-preserving SDE (VP-SDE), and the DDPM training objective is equivalent to continuous-time denoising score matching. Score-SDE generalizes the framework by providing a continuous-time view, the probability flow ODE for exact likelihood, and predictor-corrector sampling. The relationship is PR (initially independent, then unified): Ho et al. developed DDPM from the variational bound perspective, while Song et al. developed score-based models from the score matching/Langevin dynamics perspective, and the Score-SDE paper explicitly shows they are the same.

matches.explanation: DDPM's discrete forward process $q(x_t|x_{t-1}) = N(\sqrt{1-\beta_t} x_{t-1}, \beta_t I)$ is exactly the Euler-Maruyama discretization of the VP-SDE $dx = -\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)x\,dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dw$. Score-SDE proves this correspondence explicitly (TP_SDE.1). Same mathematical process, discrete vs continuous formulations.

Both define the reverse process for generation. DDPM: learned Gaussian reverse transitions $p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)$. Score-SDE: reverse-time SDE involving the score $\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$. The DDPM reverse transitions are the discretized reverse SDE with the score replaced by a neural network. Same generative process.

DDPM's noise prediction network $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ is proportional to the score function: $\epsilon_\theta \approx -\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$. Score-SDE's score network $s_\theta(x,t) \approx \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$. These are the same function up to a time-dependent scaling factor. DDPM notes this connection in Section 3.2.

DDPM's simplified objective $L_{\text{simple}} = E[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2]$ is exactly the denoising score matching objective of Score-SDE (up to the time-dependent weighting $\lambda(t)$). Both train a neural network to predict the noise/score at each noise level, and the objectives are equivalent up to a reweighting.

DDPM's explicit variational lower bound (ELBO) decomposition into per-step KL terms is specific to the discrete-time variational perspective. Score-SDE does not use this variational bound, instead relying on score matching or the probability flow ODE for likelihood.
The closed-form posterior $q(x_{t-1}|x_t, x_0)$ is specific to DDPM's discrete-time variational analysis. Score-SDE's continuous-time framework does not need this intermediate result.

DDPM's U-Net architecture details are shared in practice by Score-SDE implementations but are not a theoretical contribution of either paper. Score-SDE does not discuss architecture specifics as a contribution.
The VE-SDE (variance-exploding) formulation, which is the continuous-time limit of SMLD (Song & Ermon 2019), has no counterpart in DDPM. DDPM only corresponds to the VP-SDE.
The probability flow ODE is a major novel contribution of Score-SDE with no analogue in DDPM. It enables deterministic sampling and exact log-likelihood computation, neither of which DDPM provides.

Predictor-corrector sampling (combining SDE solver steps with Langevin correction) is a Score-SDE contribution. DDPM uses only ancestral sampling (which is a special case of the predictor without corrector).

The unification theorem showing DDPM = discretized VP-SDE and SMLD = discretized VE-SDE is the central theoretical contribution of Score-SDE. DDPM does not contain this unifying view (it preceded it).
Exact log-likelihood via the probability flow ODE and continuous normalizing flow change-of-variables is unique to Score-SDE. DDPM only provides a variational bound.

Both demonstrate state-of-the-art image generation. DDPM: FID 3.17 on CIFAR-10. Score-SDE: FID 2.20 on CIFAR-10 (improving upon DDPM with predictor-corrector sampling and continuous-time formulation). Score-SDE's results strictly improve upon DDPM's by leveraging the continuous-time framework.

unmatched_paper_a_explanations.DP_DDPM.3: Discrete-time ELBO decomposition into per-step KL terms. Specific to the variational perspective; Score-SDE uses score matching instead.
unmatched_paper_a_explanations.LP_DDPM.1: Closed-form posterior q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0). Intermediate result in discrete-time analysis not needed in continuous time.
unmatched_paper_a_explanations.DP_DDPM.6: U-Net architecture details. Shared in practice but not a theoretical contribution.

unmatched_paper_b_explanations.DP_SDE.6: VE-SDE formulation (continuous-time SMLD). DDPM only corresponds to VP-SDE.
unmatched_paper_b_explanations.DP_SDE.7: Probability flow ODE for deterministic sampling and exact likelihood. Major novel contribution.
unmatched_paper_b_explanations.DP_SDE.8: Predictor-corrector sampling framework. DDPM's ancestral sampling is a special case.

unmatched_paper_b_explanations.TP_SDE.2: Exact log-likelihood via continuous normalizing flow. Not available in DDPM.

summary: DDPM and Score-SDE are the discrete-time and continuous-time formulations of the same generative modeling framework. The forward process (noise addition), reverse process (denoising), neural network parameterization (noise prediction = score), and training objective (denoising = score matching) are all in exact correspondence, with DDPM being the Euler-Maruyama discretization of Score-SDE's VP-SDE. The papers were developed from different perspectives: DDPM from variational inference (maximizing a discrete-time ELBO), Score-SDE from score matching and Langevin dynamics. Score-SDE's major additional contributions beyond unification include: the probability flow ODE (enabling exact likelihood and deterministic sampling), the VE-SDE formulation (capturing SMLD), predictor-corrector sampling, and improved empirical results. DDPM's unique contributions are the explicit variational bound analysis and the simplified training objective that made diffusion models practical.
